title: Equus ligneus. Sinon
titleEn: The Wooden Horse and Sinon — Aeneid II.1–104
about: Book II opens in the hall at Carthage. Everyone falls silent, and Aeneas, from his high couch, begins the story Dido asked for. He calls it an unspeakable grief, one he shared in, and says that even a Greek soldier could hardly tell it dry-eyed; but if she is so eager to hear Troy's last agony, he will begin, though his mind shrinks from the memory. Worn down by the war and by the fates, the Greek leaders, after so many years, build a horse as big as a hill, plank it with cut fir, and say it is a vow for their safe return. In its dark flank they shut picked men and fill its belly with armed soldiers. Then the fleet sails out of sight and hides on a lonely shore of Tenedos. The Trojans, thinking the Greeks gone home, pour out of the gates and wander through the empty camp. They argue about the horse: Thymoetes would drag it inside the walls; Capys and the wiser heads would drown it or burn it or cut it open. Laocoön runs down from the citadel, warns them that the Greeks are not to be trusted, whatever the horse is, and hurls a spear into its side; the hollow belly groans, and only the fates, Aeneas says, kept the Trojans from tearing the hiding place open. Then Trojan shepherds drag in a bound young man, who has let himself be taken on purpose. The crowd closes round him to jeer, and Aeneas tells Dido to learn from this one man what the Greeks are. Standing before them, the prisoner cries out that neither land nor sea will have him, the Greeks having cast him off and the Trojans wanting his blood. The Trojans pity him and urge him to say who he is. He gives his name as Sinon and makes a long speech, which fills the rest of this part: he will tell the whole truth, he says, and admits he is a Greek. He tells of Palamedes, an innocent man whom the Greeks put to death, and of his own father, who sent him to serve Palamedes as a boy; of Ulysses, who pursued him once Palamedes was dead; and then breaks off, asking why he bothers to tell them this, and bids them take their vengeance at once, for Ulysses and the sons of Atreus would pay well for it.

sentences.t: Conticuere omnes, intentique ora tenebant.
sentences.l: They fell silent, all, and, intent, were holding their faces.
sentences.i: All fell silent, and they kept their faces turned toward him, intent.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a new book; Book II is the narrative Aeneas gives at Dido's request at the end of Book I, so Virgil's own voice steps back and a character speaks for nearly the whole book. 'Conticuere' = 'conticuerunt' (the -ere ending for -erunt; you'll see this constantly). 'intenti' is nominative plural, agreeing with 'omnes', which is the subject of 'tenebant' as well as of 'conticuere'. 'ora tenebant' — 'held their faces', that is, kept them fixed on the speaker; 'tenebant' is imperfect, so the silence lasts.

sentences.t: Inde toro pater Aeneas sic orsus ab alto:
sentences.l: Then from the couch father Aeneas thus began, from the high one:
sentences.i: Then father Aeneas began, from the high couch where he lay:
sentences.n: 'toro… ab alto' — 'from the high couch': 'toro' and 'alto' agree, with the preposition tucked in before the adjective. Guests at a banquet reclined on couches, and Aeneas, the guest of honour, speaks from the high one. 'pater' is Aeneas's regular title in the poem: a father, and the head of his people. 'orsus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'ordior' ('begin', used of speech or weaving), a passive form with active sense; the sentence has no verb of saying, only 'sic orsus', with the verb ('est') dropped. The colon opens his speech; Greenough prints no speech mark here.

sentences.i: Queen, you bid me live again a grief too great for words: how the Greeks tore down Troy's wealth and her kingdom, so worthy of tears;
sentences.n: 'Infandum… dolorem' — 'un-speakable', from 'for, fari' (to speak); the opening word hangs over the whole book. 'renovare' — to make new again, to relive. 'ut… eruerint' — an indirect question explaining 'dolorem' (perfect subjunctive, 'how they have overthrown'). 'Troianas opes' is wealth, resources, power; 'lamentabile' is 'worthy of lament'. 'Danai' (nominative plural) is one of the commonest names for the Greeks in the poem, after Danaus; 'Argivi', 'Achivi' and 'Pelasgi' are others, all used interchangeably.

sentences.t:
quaeque ipse miserrima vidi,
et quorum pars magna fui.
sentences.l:
and the most wretched things which I myself saw,
and of which a great part I was.
sentences.i: and the most pitiful things I saw with my own eyes, and in which I had a great share.
sentences.n: 'quaeque' = 'et quae', 'and the things which': it joins this relative clause to the 'ut' clause before it ('the grief of how… and of the things which…'). 'ipse' (I myself) claims eyewitness authority: the whole of Book II is a firsthand account. 'miserrima' is a superlative, 'most wretched'. 'quorum pars magna fui' — 'of which I was a great part': a relative clause with 'pars' as predicate.

sentences.t:
Quis talia fando
Myrmidonum Dolopumve aut duri miles Ulixi
temperet a lacrimis?
sentences.l:
Who, such things in telling, of the Myrmidons
or Dolopes, or soldier of hard Ulysses,
would keep from tears?
sentences.i: Who, in telling such things, would hold back his tears, though he were a Myrmidon or a Dolopian, or a soldier of stern Ulysses?
sentences.n: A rhetorical question. 'Quis… temperet' — present subjunctive of potential ('who would keep himself...?'), with 'a lacrimis' ('from tears'; 'temperare' takes 'a' + ablative of what one refrains from). 'talia fando' is an ablative of the gerund, 'in telling such things'. 'Myrmidonum', 'Dolopum' (here with -ve, 'or') are old genitive plurals in -um (you'll see this constantly): the Myrmidons were Achilles's men, the Dolopes were a Thessalian people who also fought for the Greeks. 'duri… Ulixi' — 'Ulixi' is the old genitive of 'Ulixes', and 'duri' agrees with it ('hard', 'stern'). The point: even Greeks would weep.

sentences.t:
Et iam nox umida caelo
praecipitat, suadentque cadentia sidera somnos.
sentences.l:
And already damp night from the sky
is rushing down, and the setting stars persuade to sleep.
sentences.i: And already dewy night is falling from the sky, and the sinking stars invite us to sleep.
sentences.n: 'Et iam' marks the lateness of the hour; 'nox umida' — night is 'moist' with dew. 'praecipitat' is intransitive here, 'plunges', a favourite verb for the setting of night or the sun. 'suadent' — 'urge, counsel' with the accusative 'somnos'. The stars 'falling' (cadentia) are the stars setting; the line suggests Aeneas could leave off, which makes his decision to go on, in the next sentence, an act of courtesy.

sentences.t:
Sed si tantus amor casus cognoscere nostros
et breviter Troiae supremum audire laborem,
quamquam animus meminisse horret, luctuque refugit,
incipiam.
sentences.l:
But if so great is the love to know our misfortunes
and briefly to hear Troy's last labour,
though my mind shrinks to remember, and flees back in grief,
I will begin.
sentences.i: But if you so much want to know our misfortunes and hear, in brief, of Troy's last ordeal, then — though my mind shudders to recall it and recoils in grief — I will begin.
sentences.n: A long conditional period: 'si tantus amor (est)… incipiam', with the 'quamquam' clause (concession, indicative) inside it. 'casus cognoscere nostros' and 'audire' are infinitives after 'amor' (a noun that takes an infinitive, 'the desire to know'). 'supremum… laborem' — 'Troy's final ordeal'. 'meminisse' is a perfect infinitive with present meaning ('to remember'). 'animus horret… refugit' — the mind bristles and flees back, a physical image. The verb comes last: 'incipiam' is the whole delay resolved at once. In Greenough's text the full stop is printed with no space after it ('incipiam.Fracti'), so the unit stops at 'incipiam.'; the next sentence begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
Fracti bello fatisque repulsi
ductores Danaum, tot iam labentibus annis,
instar montis equum divina Palladis arte
aedificant, sectaque intexunt abiete costas:
sentences.l:
Broken by war and driven back by the fates,
the leaders of the Danaans, so many years now gliding by,
build a horse the size of a mountain by the divine art of Pallas,
and weave its ribs of cut fir:
sentences.i: Broken by the war and driven back by the fates, the leaders of the Greeks, with so many years now slipping by, build a horse as huge as a mountain, by the divine skill of Pallas, and weave its ribs of sawn fir:
sentences.n: 'Fracti… repulsi' — two perfect participles, 'broken' and 'repelled', in the nominative with 'ductores'. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural (= 'Danaorum'). 'tot iam labentibus annis' — ablative absolute, 'so many years now gliding past'. 'instar montis' — 'the very image (of a mountain)', an indeclinable noun taking the genitive, 'the match of a mountain', used here to describe 'equum': a horse as big as a mountain. 'divina Palladis arte' — Pallas Athena is the divine craftswoman behind the horse. 'intexunt' — 'weave in' (like a loom); the planks are fitted in. 'secta abiete' — cut fir, in the ablative (of material or means); 'abiete' is scanned ab-je-te, the i consonantal.

sentences.t: votum pro reditu simulant;
sentences.l: a vow for their return they pretend;
sentences.i: they give it out as a vow for their safe return;
sentences.n: 'votum pro reditu' — a vow for a safe homecoming. 'simulant' — 'pretend', the first hint of the lie on which the whole story turns; Aeneas gives it away at once, looking back.

sentences.t: ea fama vagatur.
sentences.l: that report goes wandering.
sentences.i: and that is the story that spreads.
sentences.n: 'ea fama vagatur' — the rumour 'wanders' (a standard verb for rumour moving about). 'ea' agrees with 'fama'. The Trojans' mistake will be to believe it, but Aeneas does not say so yet.

sentences.t:
Huc delecta virum sortiti corpora furtim
includunt caeco lateri, penitusque cavernas
ingentis uterumque armato milite complent.
sentences.l:
Here, chosen bodies of men, drawn by lot, in secret
they shut into the dark flank, and deep the caverns
vast and the womb they fill with armed soldiery.
sentences.i: Into its dark side, in secrecy, they shut picked men chosen by lot, and fill its huge caverns and its very womb with armed soldiery.
sentences.n: 'Huc' — 'into this (horse)'. 'delecta virum… corpora' — 'chosen bodies of men'; 'virum' is the old genitive plural, 'virorum'. 'sortiti' is a deponent perfect participle (active in sense), 'having drawn lots'. 'caeco lateri' — dative of 'includere', the flank is 'blind' (dark). 'cavernas ingentis' — 'ingentis' is an accusative plural in -is (Greenough keeps these, for 'ingentes'). 'penitus' — 'deep inside'. 'uterum' — 'the womb', 'belly', a bold metaphor Virgil returns to at 38 and 52: the Greeks are an unborn brood. 'armato milite' — ablative of means after 'complent' ('fill with'), 'with armed soldiery' (a collective singular).

sentences.t:
Est in conspectu Tenedos, notissima fama
insula, dives opum, Priami dum regna manebant,
nunc tantum sinus et statio male fida carinis:
sentences.l:
There is in sight Tenedos, most famous by fame,
an island, rich in wealth while Priam's kingdoms remained,
now only a bay and an anchorage poorly faithful to ships:
sentences.i: In view lies Tenedos, an island very well known by repute, rich in resources while Priam's kingdom stood, now only a bay, and a roadstead that cannot be trusted by ships:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Tenedos is an island off the Trojan coast, within sight of the plain. 'notissima fama' — 'best known by report'. 'dum… manebant' — 'dum' with the imperfect indicative, 'as long as', 'while' (here plural 'regna' for the one kingdom, a poetic plural). 'nunc tantum' — 'now only'. 'statio male fida carinis' — 'an anchorage unfaithful to keels', that is, unsafe for ships ('statio' is a place where ships can lie at anchor). The description is of Tenedos as Aeneas knows it now, after the fall; the present tense is the speaker's present.

sentences.t: huc se provecti deserto in litore condunt.
sentences.l: hither, drawn out, on the deserted shore they hide themselves.
sentences.i: Here they sail out and hide themselves on its empty shore.
sentences.n: 'huc' — 'to this place'. 'provecti' is a perfect participle of 'provehor' (passive in form, 'carried forward'), used here of ships putting out to sea. 'deserto in litore' — the shore is empty of people, so they can hide. 'se condunt' — 'hide themselves'.

sentences.t: Nos abiisse rati et vento petiisse Mycenas:
sentences.l: We, believing them gone, and by the wind to have sought Mycenae:
sentences.i: We thought they had gone, and had sailed before the wind for Mycenae.
sentences.n: 'Nos abiisse rati' — an accusative-and-infinitive after 'rati' (deponent perfect participle of 'reor', 'having thought'), with 'eos' (the Greeks) left to be supplied; 'abiisse' and 'petiisse' are perfect infinitives of 'abeo' and 'peto' (both are -iisse forms), and the sentence has no main verb of its own. Mycenae is Agamemnon's city, standing for Greece. The colon leads into the Trojans' reaction.

sentences.t: ergo omnis longo solvit se Teucria luctu;
sentences.l: therefore all Teucria looses itself from its long grief;
sentences.i: and so all Troy shakes off its long grief;
sentences.n: 'ergo' states the consequence. 'Teucria' is the land of the Teucri, the Trojans (named for King Teucer); the whole country is the subject. 'solvit se' — 'looses itself', like a prisoner released. 'longo luctu' — ablative of separation after 'solvit se'; the long grief of the siege; the relief is brief, and Aeneas knows it.

sentences.t: panduntur portae;
sentences.l: the gates are thrown open;
sentences.i: the gates are flung wide;
sentences.n: 'panduntur' — the passive of 'pando', 'are spread open', in the present tense of vivid narrative. 'portae' is the subject; the passive names nobody as opening them.

sentences.t:
iuvat ire et Dorica castra
desertosque videre locos litusque relictum.
sentences.l:
it pleases to go, and to see the Doric camp
and the abandoned places and the shore left behind.
sentences.i: it is a joy to walk out and see the Greek camp, the deserted ground, and the shore they left.
sentences.n: 'iuvat ire… videre' — 'it pleases (us) to go… to see' (an impersonal verb with infinitives). 'Dorica' — 'Doric', from the Dorians, one of the Greek peoples, put for 'Greek'. 'desertos… locos' — 'locos' is the masculine plural of 'locus' (the plural could be 'loci' or 'loca'). 'litus relictum' — the shore they had left, now empty of ships.

sentences.t: Hic Dolopum manus, hic saevus tendebat Achilles;
sentences.l: Here the Dolopian band, here fierce Achilles pitched his tent;
sentences.i: Here the Dolopes were posted, here fierce Achilles had his quarters;
sentences.n: The Trojans walk through the camp pointing out where each contingent had been. 'tendebat' is used without an object, 'was encamped'. 'Dolopum' — old genitive plural; see line 7. 'saevus Achilles' — the standing epithet 'fierce' for the great enemy, dead by now. The repeated 'hic… hic' is the pointing of the sightseers.

sentences.t: classibus hic locus;
sentences.l: for the fleets, here, the place;
sentences.i: here the ships had their place;
sentences.n: 'classibus hic locus' — a dative of the thing the place was for, 'the place for the fleets', with 'est' understood. The sentence is a series of short, verbless statements: the Trojans are telling each other the history of the ground.

sentences.t: hic acie certare solebant.
sentences.l: here they used to fight in battle line.
sentences.i: here they used to meet us in battle.
sentences.n: 'acie certare' — 'to contend with the battle line', ablative of means or manner; 'solebant' — the imperfect of habit. With this, Aeneas ends the tour and returns to the horse.

sentences.t:
Pars stupet innuptae donum exitiale Minervae,
et molem mirantur equi;
sentences.l:
A part is amazed at the deadly gift of unwed Minerva,
and they marvel at the bulk of the horse;
sentences.i: Some stand amazed at the deadly offering to the maiden Minerva, and marvel at the bulk of the horse;
sentences.n: 'Pars stupet… mirantur' — a singular collective subject ('pars') with a plural verb in the next clause, the commonest kind of agreement by sense. 'innuptae… Minervae' — Minerva (Athena) is the unmarried goddess; the horse is supposed to be her gift. 'exitiale' — 'deadly', the sentence's secret: Aeneas, who is telling this afterwards, can say what the Trojans did not know. 'molem' is 'mass, bulk'.

sentences.t:
primusque Thymoetes
duci intra muros hortatur et arce locari,
sive dolo, seu iam Troiae sic fata ferebant.
sentences.l:
and first Thymoetes
urges that it be led within the walls and set in the citadel,
whether by guile or because by now Troy's fates were bearing it so.
sentences.i: and Thymoetes is the first to urge that it be taken inside the walls and set up on the citadel, whether from treachery or because Troy's fate was already moving that way.
sentences.n: 'primusque Thymoetes' — a Trojan, named here for the first time; 'duci' and 'locari' are present passive infinitives after 'hortatur' ('urges that it be led… placed'), with the subject accusative 'equum' understood. 'arce' — 'in the citadel' (ablative of place where, without 'in'). 'sive dolo, seu' — 'whether by guile (whose, Aeneas does not say) or because…'; 'sive… seu' are two forms of the same conjunction, varied for style. 'fata ferebant' — the fates were bearing things that way: Aeneas, looking back, gives the whole catastrophe a cause that no human could have refused.

sentences.t:
At Capys, et quorum melior sententia menti,
aut pelago Danaum insidias suspectaque dona
praecipitare iubent, subiectisque urere flammis,
aut terebrare cavas uteri et temptare latebras.
sentences.l:
But Capys, and those whose mind has the better judgment,
either into the sea the Danaans' ambush and suspect gifts
bid them hurl, and by flames set beneath burn it,
or bore through the hollow hiding places of the belly and probe them.
sentences.i: But Capys, and those with sounder minds, tell them either to throw the Greeks' trap and their suspect gift into the sea, or to burn it with fire set underneath, or to bore into the hollow hiding places of its belly and probe them.
sentences.n: 'At' sets the opposing party against Thymoetes. 'quorum melior sententia menti' — 'whose mind had a better opinion', a dative of possession ('menti' is dative of 'mens'). The verb 'iubent' has a plural subject (Capys and those with him), and the infinitives that hang on it are 'praecipitare' and 'urere' (the sea, and fire, joined by -que) and 'terebrare' and 'temptare' (cutting the horse open and probing it). 'Danaum insidias' — 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural again. 'suspecta dona' — 'gifts suspected'. 'subiectis flammis' — ablative absolute, 'fire placed under'. 'uteri' is the genitive depending on 'latebras'.

sentences.t: Scinditur incertum studia in contraria volgus.
sentences.l: The wavering crowd is split into opposite zeals.
sentences.i: The wavering crowd is torn between opposing wishes.
sentences.n: 'Scinditur… volgus' — 'volgus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgus', the common people, a neuter noun (hence 'incertum', neuter). 'studia in contraria' — 'into opposite enthusiasms', the preposition showing the direction of the split. The line closes the debate with the crowd split between the two parties.

sentences.t:
Primus ibi ante omnis, magna comitante caterva,
Laocoön ardens summa decurrit ab arce,
et procul:
sentences.l:
First there, before all, with a great throng accompanying,
Laocoön, blazing, runs down from the top of the citadel,
and from far off:
sentences.i: Foremost of all, with a great crowd accompanying him, Laocoön comes running down, ablaze with feeling, from the top of the citadel, and cries from far off:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Laocoön is a Trojan priest (Virgil says whose, later in the book); his is a Greek name, and Greenough keeps the diaeresis in 'Laocoön'. 'ante omnis' = 'ante omnes', before all. 'magna comitante caterva' — ablative absolute, 'a great crowd accompanying'. 'ardens' — burning with zeal. 'summa… ab arce' — 'from the highest part of the citadel'. 'et procul' — a dropped verb of speaking ('and he cries out from afar'), the colon bringing in the speech. The speech itself is not opened by a verb; the mark follows.

sentences.t: “O miseri, quae tanta insania, cives?
sentences.l: “O wretched ones, what so great madness, citizens?
sentences.i: “Poor wretches, citizens, what vast madness is this?
sentences.n: 'O miseri' — vocative plural: 'wretched people'. 'quae tanta insania' — 'what so great madness (is this)?', an exclamatory question with 'est' dropped. 'cives' is a vocative, in the same plural. Speech marks as printed by Greenough: opening on this unit, closing at 49.

sentences.t: Creditis avectos hostis?
sentences.l: Do you believe the enemy sailed away?
sentences.i: Do you think the enemy have sailed off?
sentences.n: 'Creditis' — a question with no particle, tone alone. 'avectos hostis' — 'hostis' is accusative plural (= 'hostes'); the accusative-and-infinitive 'avectos (esse)' follows 'creditis', so 'hostes' is subject of the infinitive: 'do you believe the enemy carried away?'. The sentence is a flat denial in the form of a question.

sentences.t:
Aut ulla putatis
dona carere dolis Danaum?
sentences.l:
Or do you think any gifts
are free of Danaan guile?
sentences.i: Or do you suppose any present from the Greeks comes free of trickery?
sentences.n: 'Aut ulla putatis' — the second member, 'or do you suppose that any…'. 'carere dolis' — 'to lack tricks', 'carere' takes the ablative. 'Danaum' is again the old genitive plural. 'Aut' opens the second question without any particle of doubt: the speaker is pressing, not asking.

sentences.t: Sic notus Ulixes?
sentences.l: Is Ulysses so known?
sentences.i: Is that how we know Ulysses?
sentences.n: 'Sic notus Ulixes?' — a clipped, ironic question: 'is this how Ulysses is known to you?', or 'is that the Ulysses we know?' Laocoön appeals to his reputation for tricks. The 'sic' is 'in this way', and 'notus' (known) has 'est' dropped.

sentences.t:
aut hoc inclusi ligno occultantur Achivi,
aut haec in nostros fabricata est machina muros
inspectura domos venturaque desuper urbi,
aut aliquis latet error;
sentences.l:
Either, shut in this wood, Achaeans are hidden,
or this engine has been built against our walls,
to look down on our houses, and to come down on the city from above,
or some trick lies hidden;
sentences.i: Either Greeks lie hidden, shut up inside this timber, or this engine has been built to overlook our houses and come down on the city from above, or some other trick is lurking;
sentences.n: 'aut… aut… aut' — three alternatives. 'inclusi ligno' — 'shut in the wood': 'ligno' is ablative, used for the wooden horse. 'Achivi' is another name for the Greeks. 'haec… machina' — 'machina' is a siege-engine. 'inspectura' and 'ventura' are future participles used for purpose ('about to look into', 'about to come'); they describe what the machine is meant to do. 'urbi' is dative, 'against the city'. 'aliquis latet error' — 'some error (deceit) lies hidden'. The three guesses end with the vague 'some error': a speaker who does not know, and only knows he fears.

sentences.t: equo ne credite, Teucri.
sentences.l: do not trust the horse, Teucrians.
sentences.i: put no faith in the horse, men of Troy.
sentences.n: 'equo ne credite' — 'ne' with the imperative, the poetic form of a prohibition ('credite', imperative plural of 'credo', which takes the dative 'equo'). 'Teucri' is vocative plural, 'Trojans', after their ancestor Teucer.

sentences.t: Quicquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentis.”
sentences.l: Whatever it is, I fear the Danaans, and them bringing gifts.”
sentences.i: Whatever this thing is, I am afraid of the Greeks, even when it is presents that they bring.”
sentences.n: A line often quoted, and easy to misread. 'Quicquid id est' — 'whatever it is' (Greenough prints 'Quicquid'; many editions print 'quidquid'). 'timeo Danaos et dona ferentis' — 'ferentis' = 'ferentes', a present participle in the accusative plural agreeing with 'Danaos'; 'et' is best taken as 'even' — 'the Greeks, and (them) even when they bring gifts'. Laocoön does not say 'beware the gifts' but 'I fear the men'. The closing speech mark ends the speech that began at 42.

sentences.t:
Sic fatus, validis ingentem viribus hastam
in latus inque feri curvam compagibus alvum
contorsit:
sentences.l:
So having spoken, with strong strength a huge spear
into the flank and into the curved belly of the beast, with its joinings,
he hurled:
sentences.i: Having spoken so, he hurled with mighty strength a huge spear into the creature's side, into the belly curved with its jointed timbers:
sentences.n: 'Sic fatus' — 'having spoken thus', a perfect participle of the deponent 'for' (to speak) used as a stock formula of the narrative. 'validis ingentem viribus hastam' — hyperbaton: the adjective 'validis' goes with 'viribus', 'ingentem' with 'hastam', and the two phrases interlock. 'feri' (genitive) is the horse, 'beast' (as a monster); 'compagibus' (ablative) is 'with its joints', the planks fitted together. The sentence runs through the lines and puts the verb 'contorsit' (he hurled) at the end, like the spear in flight.

sentences.t:
stetit illa tremens, uteroque recusso
insonuere cavae gemitumque dedere cavernae.
sentences.l:
it stood, quivering, and, the womb shaken,
the hollow caverns resounded and gave a groan.
sentences.i: The spear stood quivering, and as the belly shook, the hollow chambers rang and gave out a groan.
sentences.n: 'stetit illa tremens' — the spear stuck in the wood and shook. 'utero recusso' — ablative absolute, 'the belly having been shaken back' ('recutio', to cause to rebound). 'insonuere' = 'insonuerunt', the -ere perfect again. 'gemitum dedere' = 'gemitum dederunt', 'gave a groan' (another -ere form): the hollow belly answers with a groan; Aeneas, telling it afterwards, knows what is inside, but the Trojans do not.

sentences.t:
Et, si fata deum, si mens non laeva fuisset,
impulerat ferro Argolicas foedare latebras,
Troiaque, nunc stares, Priamique arx alta, maneres.
sentences.l:
And, if the fates of the gods, if the mind had not been perverse,
he had urged us to defile with iron the Argive hiding places,
and, Troy, you would now stand, and you, Priam's high citadel, would remain.
sentences.i: And if the fates of the gods, and our own minds, had not been against us, he would have driven us to rip open that Greek hiding place with the sword, and you, Troy, would still stand, and Priam's high citadel would still be here.
sentences.n: Aeneas, in hindsight, turns to address Troy itself ('Troia… stares'): an apostrophe. The sentence is a mixed conditional: 'si fata deum, si mens non laeva fuisset' (pluperfect subjunctive; after 'si fata deum' the verb is left out, '[had not been against us]'), 'impulerat' (pluperfect indicative for 'impulisset'; the indicative makes the result vivid, 'he had all but driven us'; the subject is Laocoön), and 'stares… maneres' (imperfect subjunctive, 'you would now be standing'). 'deum' is the old genitive plural of 'deus' (= 'deorum'). 'laeva' — literally 'left', here 'perverse, ill-judging'. 'foedare' — 'to defile, to mar', here with the spear ('ferro', 'iron'). Greenough prints 'stares' (second person, addressing Troy); the Latin Library has 'staret', which would make it a statement about Troy in the third person.

sentences.t:
Ecce, manus iuvenem interea post terga revinctum
pastores magno ad regem clamore trahebant
Dardanidae, qui se ignotum venientibus ultro,
hoc ipsum ut strueret Troiamque aperiret Achivis,
obtulerat, fidens animi atque in utrumque paratus,
sentences.l:
Behold, as to the hands, a young man, meanwhile, behind the back bound,
shepherds to the king with great shouting were dragging,
Dardans, who, unknown, to those coming, of his own accord,
in order to work this very thing and open Troy to the Achaeans,
had offered himself, confident in heart and ready for either course,
sentences.i: Meanwhile, look, Dardan shepherds were dragging before the king, with a great uproar, a young man whose hands were tied behind his back, who had put himself in the way of the newcomers, a stranger and of his own will, so as to bring this very thing about and open Troy to the Greeks, sure of his nerve and ready either way,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ecce' — 'look!', a sudden turn, the narrator's pointing. 'manus… revinctum' — 'bound as to the hands': 'manus' is an accusative of respect (a Greek-style construction) with the participle, and 'iuvenem' is the object of 'trahebant'; 'pastores' is the subject, 'Dardanidae' in apposition. 'Dardanidae' — 'sons of Dardanus', the Trojans. 'magno ad regem clamore' — 'to the king with great shouting' ('magno' goes with 'clamore'; 'regem' is Priam). 'qui se… obtulerat' — 'qui' refers to the young man; 'ignotum' agrees with 'se'. 'hoc ipsum ut strueret… aperiret' — purpose clauses. 'fidens animi' — a genitive of respect ('confident in spirit'). 'in utrumque paratus' — 'ready for either'. The long sentence is divided at the comma because it would exceed five lines; the unit ends at 'paratus,' and the last pair of alternatives forms the next unit.

sentences.t: seu versare dolos, seu certae occumbere morti.
sentences.l: either to ply tricks or to fall to certain death.
sentences.i: either to ply his tricks or to meet a sure death.
sentences.n: 'seu versare dolos, seu… occumbere morti' — 'whether to turn over his tricks, or to fall to sure death'; the dative with 'occumbere' ('fall to death') is standard for this verb. 'certae… morti' — 'sure death', that is, death that cannot be avoided if his trick fails. The two alternatives are Sinon's two possible courses, to go on with his tricks or to die, and the young man is ready for both.

sentences.t:
Undique visendi studio Troiana iuventus
circumfusa ruit, certantque inludere capto.
sentences.l:
From all sides in eagerness to see, the Trojan youth
pour round him, and vie to mock the captive.
sentences.i: From every side, eager to see him, the young men of Troy pour round and compete to jeer at their prisoner.
sentences.n: 'visendi studio' — 'by eagerness of seeing': a gerund in the genitive. 'circumfusa' is a perfect participle, 'poured around'. 'ruit' — 'rushes', in the singular for the collective 'iuventus'; then 'certant' (plural). 'inludere capto' — 'to mock the captive': 'inludere' (= 'illudere') takes the dative.

sentences.t:
Accipe nunc Danaum insidias, et crimine ab uno
disce omnes.
sentences.l:
Hear now the Danaans' ambushes, and from one crime
learn all.
sentences.i: Hear now the treacheries of the Greeks, and from one charge of crime learn what they all are.
sentences.n: Aeneas turns to Dido: 'Accipe' is addressed to her ('hear now'). 'crimine ab uno disce omnes' — a famous phrase: 'from one crime learn all', the particular standing for the whole. 'crimine ab uno' — 'from one charge' (or 'crime'). 'disce' — imperative. The line closes the paragraph, with the next beginning the story of Sinon.

sentences.t:
Namque ut conspectu in medio turbatus, inermis
constitit atque oculis Phrygia agmina circumspexit:
sentences.l:
For as, in the middle of the sight, confused, unarmed,
he stood, and with his eyes looked around the Phrygian lines:
sentences.i: For when he stood there in full view, bewildered and unarmed, and looked round with his eyes at the ranks of Phrygians:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Namque ut' — 'for when', 'ut' with the perfect indicative ('constitit… circumspexit') means 'when, as soon as'. 'in medio conspectu' — in the open, in the sight of all. 'Phrygia' means Trojan ('Phrygian' is a poetic word for Trojan). 'circumspexit' — the perfect of 'circumspicio'. The colon brings in Sinon's speech.

sentences.t:
“Heu, quae nunc tellus inquit quae me aequora possunt
accipere?
sentences.l:
“Alas, what land now, said he, what seas can
receive me?
sentences.i: “Alas, what earth is there now, he says, what waters able to take me in?
sentences.n: The speech begins with 'inquit' set into it, with no commas around it in Greenough's printing (as printed: 'Heu, quae nunc tellus inquit quae me aequora possunt'); the effect is a single breath of despair. 'Heu' — an interjection of grief. 'possunt accipere' — 'can receive'. The opening mark is on this unit.

sentences.t:
Aut quid iam misero mihi denique restat,
cui neque apud Danaos usquam locus, et super ipsi
Dardanidae infensi poenas cum sanguine poscunt?”
sentences.l:
Or what, now, is left to wretched me at last,
to whom there is no place anywhere among the Danaans, and in addition the very
Dardans, hostile, demand my punishment with my blood?”
sentences.i: Or what, in the end, is left to a wretch like me, who have no place anywhere among the Greeks, and for whom, besides, the Trojans themselves, in their hatred, demand a penalty paid in blood?”
sentences.n: 'quid… restat' — 'what is left?'. 'misero mihi' — dative of the person affected. 'cui' is a relative with a dative of possession: 'to whom there is no place'. 'neque apud Danaos usquam locus' — no place among the Greeks anywhere (with 'est' understood). 'et super' — 'and in addition' (the preposition used as an adverb). 'ipsi Dardanidae infensi' — 'the Dardans themselves, hostile'. 'poenas cum sanguine poscunt' — 'poenas poscere' means to demand punishment; 'cum sanguine' is 'with blood', that is, in blood. The closing mark ends this speech.

sentences.t:
Quo gemitu conversi animi, compressus et omnis
impetus.
sentences.l:
At that groan our minds were turned, and all
the onset was checked.
sentences.i: At that groan our hearts were moved, and all our fury was checked.
sentences.n: 'Quo gemitu' — a connecting relative (= 'et eo gemitu'), 'at which groan' (a form you'll see constantly). 'conversi animi' — the minds are 'turned', changed from anger to pity. 'compressus' (est) is a perfect passive, 'was pressed down'. Aeneas now speaks as one of the Trojans ('we').

sentences.t: Hortamur fari;
sentences.l: We urge him to speak;
sentences.i: We urge him to speak;
sentences.n: 'Hortamur fari' — 'we urge (him) to speak'; 'fari' is the present infinitive of the deponent 'for'. The object 'eum' is dropped.

sentences.t:
quo sanguine cretus,
quidve ferat, memoret, quae sit fiducia capto.
sentences.l:
from what blood sprung, or what he brings, let him tell,
what confidence the captive has.
sentences.i: to tell what blood he comes of, what he brings, and what a prisoner has to trust in.
sentences.n: A series of indirect clauses hanging on 'hortamur fari' and 'memoret': 'quo sanguine cretus' (with 'sit' understood: 'sprung from what blood'), 'quidve ferat' ('or what he brings', an indirect question, subjunctive), 'memoret' ('let him tell', a subjunctive of indirect command with no 'ut') and 'quae sit fiducia' ('what ground of confidence there is'). The first two clauses are joined by the enclitic '-ve' ('or'); the last has no connective (asyndeton). 'cretus' is the participle of 'cresco', here 'born of'. 'capto' is dative: 'for a prisoner'.

sentences.t: [Ille haec, deposita tandem formidine, fatur:]
sentences.l: [He, these things, his fear at last laid aside, says:]
sentences.i: [Then, his fear at last put aside, he spoke as follows:]
sentences.n: A bracketed line: Greenough prints II.76 in square brackets as spurious (that is, in his judgment not Virgil's). It is kept as its own unit and printed in brackets as in the edition; the Latin Library does not print it at all. It only introduces Sinon's reply. 'Ille' is Sinon. 'deposita… formidine' — ablative absolute, 'fear laid aside'. 'fatur' is the historic present of the deponent 'for'.

sentences.t:
“Cuncta equidem tibi, Rex, fuerit quodcumque, fatebor
vera, inquit;
sentences.l:
“All things indeed to you, King, whatever it shall be, I will confess
true, he says;
sentences.i: “All of it, King, I will tell you true, whatever it turns out to be, he says;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Cuncta… vera… fatebor' — 'all things true… I will confess': 'cuncta' and 'vera' go together (adjective and noun split around 'tibi, Rex, fuerit quodcumque'). 'equidem' — 'for my part, indeed'. 'Rex' is Priam. 'fuerit quodcumque' — future perfect, 'whatever it shall have been', 'whatever it turns out to be'. 'inquit' comes in the middle of the speech (as with 'inquit' at 69): the speech does not stop for the tag, and the mark stays on the first unit only. The unit ends at the semicolon after 'inquit'.

sentences.t: neque me Argolica de gente negabo:
sentences.l: and I shall not deny that I am of Argive stock:
sentences.i: and I will not deny that I am of Argive stock:
sentences.n: 'neque me Argolica de gente negabo' — 'I will not deny myself to be from the Argive race'. 'negabo' takes the accusative-and-infinitive, with 'me' as subject and 'esse' dropped. Sinon's strategy is to confess the true thing first, which is that he is a Greek.

sentences.t: hoc primum;
sentences.l: this first;
sentences.i: this first of all;
sentences.n: 'hoc primum' — 'this first': he puts first what he is about to admit, with the verb ("I say") left out.

sentences.t:
nec, si miserum Fortuna Sinonem
finxit, vanum etiam mendacemque improba finget.
sentences.l:
nor, if Fortune has made wretched Sinon,
will she also make him vain and a liar, the wicked one.
sentences.i: and if Fortune has made Sinon wretched, she will not, wicked as she is, make him a liar and a cheat besides.
sentences.n: 'Sinonem' is the first time the prisoner is named. 'nec, si… finxit, … finget' — a condition with a future-looking apodosis: 'if Fortune has made X, she will not make Y'. 'finxit… finget' — the same verb twice, 'fingere', to shape or make: Fortune may fashion him wretched, but not false. 'improba' (nominative) agrees with 'Fortuna'. The irony, for the reader and for Aeneas telling it, is that Sinon is lying throughout. 'vanum… mendacemque' — 'vain' here means 'false'.

sentences.t:
Fando aliquod si forte tuas pervenit ad auris
Belidae nomen Palamedis et incluta fama
gloria, quem falsa sub proditione Pelasgi
insontem infando indicio, quia bella vetabat,
demisere neci, nunc cassum lumine lugent.
sentences.l:
If by chance in telling any name has come to your ears
of Palamedes the Belid's name, and his glory, famed by report,
whom, under a false charge of treason, the Pelasgians,
innocent, by an infamous accusation, because he opposed the war,
sent down to death, now bereft of light they mourn.
sentences.i: If the name of Palamedes, Belus's descendant, has ever happened to reach your ears in the telling, and the glory of his renown, whom the Greeks, on a false charge of treason, sent innocent to his death by a wicked accusation because he spoke against the war, and now, with him dead, they grieve.
sentences.n: 'Fando' — ablative of the gerund, 'by telling', 'by hearsay'. 'si forte… pervenit' — 'if by chance… has reached', indicative. 'Belidae' — a patronymic (genitive): descendant of Belus. Palamedes was a Greek hero; according to the later legend he exposed Ulysses's pretended madness to avoid the war, and Ulysses later had him framed as a traitor. The story is not in Homer. 'Pelasgi' — another name for the Greeks. 'falsa sub proditione' — 'under a false charge of treason'. 'insontem' — 'guiltless'. 'infando indicio' — an 'unspeakable' (wicked) information laid against him. 'demisere neci' = 'demiserunt neci' (the -ere perfect); 'neci' is a dative of 'nex'. 'cassum lumine' — 'deprived of light', a euphemism for dead. The conditional is never completed: Sinon breaks off the 'if' and goes straight into the story (anacoluthon).

sentences.t:
Illi me comitem et consanguinitate propinquum
pauper in arma pater primis huc misit ab annis,
dum stabat regno incolumis regumque vigebat
consiliis, et nos aliquod nomenque decusque
gessimus.
sentences.l:
To him, as companion and close in kinship,
my father, poor, to arms sent me hither from my first years,
while he stood safe in the realm and flourished in the
counsels of kings, and we also some name and glory
bore.
sentences.i: To him, as his comrade and near by blood, my father, a poor man, sent me here to the war from my earliest years, while he stood unharmed in the realm and carried weight in the councils of kings, and I too held some name and honour.
sentences.n: 'Illi me comitem… misit' — 'illi' is Palamedes: 'to him, me as companion… sent', a deliberately Latin order. 'consanguinitate propinquum' — 'close by blood', an ablative of respect. 'in arma' — 'into war'. 'primis ab annis' — 'from the first years'. 'dum stabat… vigebat' — 'dum' with the imperfect indicative, 'while'; the subject is Palamedes, not the father: safe in the realm and strong in the counsels of kings. 'consiliis' — 'councils'. 'nos… gessimus' — 'we too bore name and honour': 'nos' is most likely Sinon speaking of himself, the plural for the singular. 'aliquod' agrees with 'nomen'.

sentences.t:
Invidia postquam pellacis Ulixi—
haud ignota loquor—superis concessit ab oris,
adflictus vitam in tenebris luctuque trahebam,
et casum insontis mecum indignabar amici.
sentences.l:
After, through the envy of the wily Ulysses —
I speak not unknown things — he departed from the upper shores,
I, afflicted, dragged my life in darkness and grief,
and over the fate of my innocent friend I raged with myself.
sentences.i: But after he withdrew from the world above, through the envy of crafty Ulysses (I speak of nothing unknown), I dragged out my life in gloom and mourning, cast down, and raged to myself at the fate of my innocent friend.
sentences.n: A parenthesis set off by dashes: 'haud ignota loquor' — 'I am saying nothing unknown', that is, 'you know this story'. 'Invidia postquam pellacis Ulixi' — 'Ulixi' is the old genitive of 'Ulixes'. 'superis concessit ab oris' — a euphemism: he 'withdrew from the upper shores', that is, he died. 'pellacis' — 'deceitful'. 'adflictus' — 'cast down', from 'affligo'. 'luctu' is ablative. 'casum insontis… amici' — 'the fall of my innocent friend'. 'mecum indignabar' — 'I raged with myself', that is, inwardly; the anger is at the fate of his friend. Sinon sets himself up as the loyal friend of the victim.

sentences.t:
Nec tacui demens, et me, fors si qua tulisset,
si patrios umquam remeassem victor ad Argos,
promisi ultorem, et verbis odia aspera movi.
sentences.i: Nor did I keep quiet, like a madman: I promised to avenge him myself if any chance should bring it about, if ever I came home a victor to my native Argos, and with these words I stirred up bitter hatred.
sentences.n: 'demens' — in apposition with the subject, 'madly, like a fool'. 'fors si qua tulisset' — a pluperfect subjunctive in a conditional inside the reported promise, standing for the future perfect of his original words ('if chance shall bring it'). 'remeassem' = 'remeavissem' (likewise standing for the future perfect). 'victor' is a nominative, predicate. 'me… ultorem' — 'promisi' takes 'me' as the subject of an understood 'fore' ('I promised that I would be an avenger'). 'verbis odia aspera movi' — 'I stirred sharp hatreds with words'. The speech of an inexperienced man, he says, who ruined himself by talking.

sentences.t:
Hinc mihi prima mali labes, hinc semper Ulixes
criminibus terrere novis, hinc spargere voces
in volgum ambiguas, et quaerere conscius arma.
sentences.l:
From this the first stain of evil to me, from this ever Ulysses
with new accusations to terrify, from this to scatter ambiguous
words among the crowd, and to seek weapons, conscious.
sentences.i: From this came my first taint of misfortune: from this Ulysses was always frightening me with fresh charges, from this scattering ambiguous rumours among the people, and seeking arms, knowing what he did.
sentences.n: 'Hinc… hinc… hinc' — three repeated 'from this', an anaphora. 'mali labes' — 'labes' is a slip, a fall, a stain: here the first taint of ruin. The second and third clauses use historic infinitives ('terrere', 'spargere', 'quaerere'), which stand in for finite verbs in vivid narrative (in the imperfect sense, 'kept terrifying', 'kept spreading'); you'll see this repeatedly. 'in volgum' — 'volgum' is Greenough's spelling of the accusative of 'vulgus', here treated as masculine (at 39 it is neuter). 'ambiguas' — 'double-meaning'. 'conscius' — 'knowingly' (of Ulysses, who knows his own guilt). 'arma' — means, weapons, a figurative sense.

sentences.t: Nec requievit enim, donec, Calchante ministro—
sentences.l: For he did not rest, until, Calchas as his instrument—
sentences.i: For he did not rest until, with Calchas as his tool—
sentences.n: 'Nec requievit enim' — 'enim' here explains and carries on the story ('for he did not rest'). 'Calchante ministro' — ablative absolute: 'Calchas being the servant'. Calchas is the Greeks' seer, whom (as Sinon's tale goes on) Ulysses used against him. The dash is Sinon's break-off: the sentence is left unfinished, as he pretends not to be able to say it.

sentences.t: sed quid ego haec autem nequiquam ingrata revolvo?
sentences.l: but why do I, in vain, unwelcome, go over these things?
sentences.i: but why do I go back over these things, to no purpose, and unwelcome?
sentences.n: 'sed quid' — 'but why?'. 'haec autem nequiquam ingrata revolvo' — 'autem' adds the turn; 'nequiquam' is 'in vain', 'ingrata' (neuter plural accusative, 'unwelcome things'). 'revolvo' — 'roll back'. The question is a stage-pause: Sinon pretends to see the uselessness of his story.

sentences.t:
Quidve moror, si omnis uno ordine habetis Achivos,
idque audire sat est?
sentences.l:
Or why do I delay, if you hold all the Achaeans in one rank,
and it is enough to hear this?
sentences.i: Or why do I linger, if you reckon all Greeks as of one stamp, and it is enough to hear that?
sentences.n: 'Quidve moror' — 'or why do I delay?' (the enclitic '-ve' = 'or'). 'si omnis uno ordine habetis Achivos' — 'omnis' = 'omnes' (the accusative plural in -is); 'uno ordine habetis' — 'you hold (them) in one class', 'you rank them all the same'. 'idque audire sat est' — 'sat' = 'satis'. This echoes the maxim at 65–66, 'disce omnes': the Trojans (Sinon suggests) already think all Greeks the same, so there is no need to tell more.

sentences.t:
Iamdudum sumite poenas,
hoc Ithacus velit, et magno mercentur Atridae.”
sentences.l:
At once take your penalties,
the Ithacan would wish this, and the Atridae would buy it dear.”
sentences.i: Take your vengeance now, at once; that is what the Ithacan would want, and the sons of Atreus would pay a great price for it.”
sentences.n: 'Iamdudum' — 'long since', 'this very moment'; 'sumite poenas' — 'exact punishment', imperative. 'Ithacus' — Ulysses, king of Ithaca. 'velit' — a potential subjunctive, 'would wish'. 'mercentur' — 'would buy' (a present indicative where English wants a conditional: vivid, 'are ready to buy'). 'magno' — ablative of price ('at a great price'). 'Atridae' — Agamemnon and Menelaus, the sons of Atreus. The closing mark is Greenough's: Sinon's long speech, begun at 77, ends here.
